lesson.title: Obamacare: Rewriting the Rules of Health Insurance
lesson.summary: Signed into law in March 2010, the Affordable Care Act was the largest expansion of American health care access since the creation of Medicare and Medicaid in 1965, using market reforms, subsidies, and an expanded Medicaid program to sharply reduce the number of uninsured Americans.
lesson.body:
When President Lyndon Johnson signed Medicare and Medicaid into law in 1965, the federal government took on direct responsibility for health coverage for the elderly and for many low income Americans, but tens of millions of working age Americans remained without any guaranteed way to get health insurance. Barack Obama had campaigned in 2008 on addressing that gap, and in March 2010, after a long and bruising legislative fight, he signed the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, commonly known as the Affordable Care Act or Obamacare, into law without a single Republican vote in Congress.

Rather than creating a government run insurance system, the Affordable Care Act built on the existing private insurance market and expanded the reach of Medicaid, the joint federal state program that had been serving low income Americans since 1965. It prohibited insurance companies from denying coverage or charging higher prices to people with pre existing medical conditions, allowed young adults to remain on a parent's insurance plan until age 26, created online marketplaces where individuals could shop for and compare private insurance plans, offered subsidies to help lower and middle income people afford coverage, and required most Americans to carry insurance or pay a penalty, a provision known as the individual mandate. It also gave states the option to expand Medicaid eligibility to more low income adults, with the federal government covering most of the added cost.

The law faced intense and sustained political opposition from Republicans, who attempted to repeal it dozens of times in Congress over the following years, and it was challenged repeatedly in the courts. In the 2012 case National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius, the Supreme Court upheld the individual mandate as a valid use of Congress's taxing power but ruled that the federal government could not force states to expand Medicaid, leaving that choice to each state and creating significant gaps in coverage between states that expanded Medicaid and those that did not. A later case, King v. Burwell in 2015, upheld the law's subsidies for people who bought insurance through the federal marketplace.

In the years after it took effect, the uninsured rate in the United States fell substantially, extending coverage to millions of Americans who had previously gone without it, even as critics continued to raise concerns about rising premiums in some markets and the complexity of the law's rules. Whatever one's view of its costs and benefits, the Affordable Care Act stood as the most significant change to American health policy since Medicare and Medicaid nearly a half century earlier, and it remained a central and unresolved battleground in American politics for years after Obama left office.
